title: 1RM Back Squat Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Free 1RM back squat calculator using Epley formula. Quickly estimate your max lift for strength training.
intro: The back squat 1RM is the single most useful number a lifter can carry around — it sets the loading for every working set, picks meet attempts, and benchmarks whether your last training block actually moved the needle. This estimator runs your top set (weight × reps) through the **Epley equation**, `1RM = w × (1 + r/30)`, the same predictor used by Wendler's 5/3/1, Sheiko templates, and most coach spreadsheets. Two other equations get cited a lot: **Brzycki** (`w × 36/(37 − r)`), which trims a couple of pounds off Epley and tends to match true singles better at 6+ reps, and **Lombardi** (`w × r^0.10`), which overshoots once you push past 8. None of these care whether you squat high-bar Olympic style or low-bar powerlifting — but your numbers will. Low-bar usually moves 5–12% more weight than high-bar for a trained lifter, so plug in whichever stance you actually compete in. For reference points: ExRx and Stronger by Science strength standards put a **novice** male squat (200 lb bodyweight) around **230 lb**, an **intermediate** lifter around **315 lb**, **advanced** around **405 lb**, and **elite/competitive** at **500 lb+**. For women at 145 lb bodyweight, those bands run roughly 125 / 175 / 235 / 290 lb. Use the calculator to set your next training cycle without having to grind a true single under a bar that hates you.
keyTakeaway: **1RM = Weight (kg) × (1 + Reps / 30)** — e.g., 100 kg × 8 reps → 1RM ≈ 127 kg; use 3–6 rep sets for the most accurate predictions (±2–5%).
useCases: Picking USAPL or USPA meet attempts from training PRs — opener at 90–92% of your estimated 1RM (e.g., 405 lb predicted → 365 lb opener), second at 96–98% (390 lb), third at 100–103% (405–415 lb) so you don't bomb out on squat

Setting your training max (TM) for Wendler 5/3/1 — Jim's rule is **TM = 85–90% of estimated 1RM**, so a 500 lb predicted squat runs the cycle off a 425–450 lb TM (Week 3 top set: 95% TM = 405–428 lb × 1+ AMRAP)
Running a peak strength block at 85–95% 1RM (heavy doubles and singles in the 4 weeks before a meet) without a true max test eating recovery you don't have
Programming a hypertrophy phase at 65–75% 1RM for 8–12 rep sets — e.g., 405 lb 1RM → 265–305 lb working sets for 4×10 quad-focused volume
Sanity-checking a recent paused squat PR — if you grind out 315 × 5 paused, that's a ~365 lb paused 1RM; comparing it to your touch-and-go 1RM tells you how much your stretch reflex is buying you
Tracking Bulgarian-method daily max work — re-estimating projected 1RM weekly from your daily top single + back-off rep work, so you can spot stagnation before it becomes overreaching

explanation:
## The Math — Epley, Brzycki, Lombardi

All three formulas take the same two inputs (weight on the bar, reps completed at or near failure) and spit out a predicted single. They disagree most at high reps:

```
Epley   (1985):  1RM = w × (1 + r/30)
Brzycki (1993):  1RM = w × 36 / (37 − r)
Lombardi(1989):  1RM = w × r^0.10
O'Conner(1989):  1RM = w × (1 + 0.025r)
```

**Worked example — 315 lb × 5 reps (a respectable intermediate top set):**
```
Epley   : 315 × (1 + 5/30)   = 315 × 1.1667 = 367.5 lb
Brzycki : 315 × 36/(37 − 5)  = 315 × 1.125  = 354.4 lb
Lombardi: 315 × 5^0.10       = 315 × 1.1746 = 370.0 lb
O'Conner: 315 × (1 + 0.125)  = 315 × 1.125  = 354.4 lb
```

That spread — about 13 lb — is normal. For 3–5 rep sets the formulas converge within 2–3%. For sets above 8 reps Lombardi will overshoot by 5–10% and Brzycki tends to be the most honest.

## Bar Position Changes The Number

The back squat is two different lifts depending on bar placement. A **high-bar (Olympic) squat** sits on the upper traps, drives more knee flexion, and gives the quads more work. A **low-bar (powerlifting) squat** sits across the rear delts on top of the spine of the scapula, opens the hip more, and shortens the moment arm at the knee. For most trained lifters this means:

- **Low-bar 1RM is 5–12% higher than high-bar 1RM** (Stronger by Science survey data and Greg Nuckols' analyses).
- If you train high-bar but plan to compete USAPL/USPA, multiply your estimated high-bar 1RM by **~1.08** for a rough low-bar target — then test it.
- The reverse adjustment matters too: a 500 lb low-bar competitor probably high-bars 445–475 lb on a good day.

## Depth — What Counts

Depth standards vary by federation, and they directly affect what 1RM you can actually use:

| Standard | Definition | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Parallel | Top of the knee level with the hip crease | USAPL, USPA, IPF (referee call) |
| Full depth (ATG) | Hamstrings on calves, hip well below knee | Olympic weightlifting, CrossFit Open |
| High squat | Hip above knee crease | Gym only; would be red-lighted in any meet |

A red light at a USAPL meet for high squat doesn't care that your bar speed was perfect — the lift doesn't count. When estimating a meet 1RM, only count reps that would pass a sanctioned judge.

## %1RM / Reps Reference Table

Useful for plugging into 5/3/1, Sheiko, Conjugate, or any percentage-based template:

| % of 1RM | Reps in Reserve (RPE) | Typical Reps |
|---|---|---|
| 100% | RPE 10 — true max | 1 |
| 95%  | RPE 9             | 2 |
| 92.5%| RPE 8.5           | 3 |
| 90%  | RPE 8             | 3–4 |
| 87.5%| RPE 7.5           | 4–5 |
| 85%  | RPE 7             | 5–6 |
| 80%  | RPE 6.5           | 6–8 |
| 75%  | RPE 6             | 8–10 |
| 70%  | RPE 5             | 10–12 |
| 65%  | RPE 4             | 12–15 |

## Programming — What Coaches Actually Do With This Number

**Wendler 5/3/1** runs every cycle off a Training Max set at 85–90% of estimated 1RM. Week 3 top set is 95% TM × 1+ (an AMRAP). You re-estimate 1RM each cycle off that AMRAP using Epley and add 5 lb to TM if it beat your previous projection.

**Sheiko #29 / #32** is volume-heavy and runs squat days at 70–85% of 1RM for sets of 2–5 reps. Total reps per session at >70% can exceed 30 — accurate 1RM input matters a lot or the volume buries you.

**Bulgarian method (Abadjiev / John Broz)** ditches percentages and asks for a daily heavy single, then back-off doubles. Estimated 1RM still matters for setting back-off load (usually 85–90% of the day's top single).

**Smolov base cycle** is famously brutal: 4 squat sessions/week, percentages built off a fresh 1RM (Mon 70%×9 sets, Wed 75%, Fri 80%, Sat 85%). Plug a stale or inflated 1RM into Smolov and you'll quit by Week 2.

## Common Errors

1. **AMRAP wasn't actually AMRAP.** If you stop a top set with 2–3 reps in reserve, Epley underprojects your max. Push the test set to where the next rep would have failed (slow concentric, breakdown in bar path) — that's RPE 9.5–10.

2. **No spotter, no safeties, no pace.** Testing a 5RM with safeties set too low or without pins is how lifters end up pinned. Set the safeties at the bottom of your squat, use a power rack, and have a competent spot. If neither is available, cap the test at 5RM and trust the math.

3. **Butt wink and lost depth.** A rep that loses lumbar position at the bottom isn't the same rep as the one you'll do under a heavier load. If your last 2 reps had a visible posterior pelvic tilt at the bottom, treat the set as 1–2 reps lighter than what you logged.

4. **Knees caving (valgus collapse).** Even a small inward knee drift on the last rep means you ran out of glute/abductor support. The 1RM estimate is still mathematically correct, but the actual single will likely miss because the load that triggered the collapse will trigger it harder on a true max.

5. **Pre-meet test too close to the platform.** Don't test a true 1RM in the last 14 days before a sanctioned meet. The CNS cost wrecks attempt selection. Use a 3RM or 5RM at 4–6 weeks out and let Epley do the rest.

6. **Comparing across belt/no-belt/wraps.** A belted, sleeved low-bar squat can be 10–20 lb above an unbelted high-bar single. Tag your training max with the gear used or you'll set the wrong opener.

faq.q: What's a strong back squat for a 200 lb man?
faq.a: Going by ExRx and Symmetric Strength standards at 200 lb bodyweight: **novice ~230 lb**, **intermediate ~315 lb**, **advanced ~405 lb**, **elite/competitive ~500 lb+**. A 1.5× bodyweight squat (300 lb) is the common 'recreational lifter' marker; 2× bodyweight (405 lb) is the line a lot of people aim at before stepping on a platform. Top-end USAPL 93 kg (205 lb) class squats sit around 700–800 lb raw.

faq.q: What's a strong squat for a woman at 145 lb bodyweight?
faq.a: Same source bands: **novice ~125 lb**, **intermediate ~175 lb**, **advanced ~235 lb**, **elite ~290 lb**. A 2× bodyweight squat (290 lb) at 145 lb places a female lifter very competitively at a USAPL 63–69 kg meet. Marisa Inda and Stefi Cohen sit well above that — but that's pro territory, not a benchmark.

faq.q: How often should I squat — every week, twice a week, daily?
faq.a: Depends on the program. Wendler 5/3/1: **once a week** heavy plus a lighter day. Texas Method: **3× per week** (volume Monday, light Wednesday, intensity Friday). Sheiko: **2–3 squat sessions/week** with volume distributed. Bulgarian/Broz method: **daily**, but only people with bulletproof recovery and no day jobs survive that long-term. For most intermediate US lifters, **2 sessions/week** (one heavy, one volume) hits the sweet spot.

faq.q: Why does my calculated 1RM feel way too high when I actually try it?
faq.a: Three usual culprits. (1) The test set wasn't true AMRAP — you left reps on the bar, so Epley overprojected. (2) You tested fresh and tried the 1RM cold or after fatigue. (3) Bar position changed: you tested high-bar in training but tried a low-bar single (or vice versa). Recompute from a 3RM, fully warm up (45–60 min), and match bar position.

faq.q: Why does my calculated 1RM feel way too low?
faq.a: Usually means you have more than 2 reps in reserve on the test set, or you're testing while still in a high-volume block (Sheiko, Smolov base). CNS fatigue blunts top-end strength even when 5RM looks fine. Take a deload week, retest a 3RM, and Epley will line up much closer to a true single.

faq.q: What's the typical high-bar to low-bar squat ratio?
faq.a: Most trained lifters move **5–12% more weight low-bar than high-bar**. So a 405 lb high-bar squat usually translates to about 425–455 lb low-bar after the technique is dialed in. The gap is bigger for taller lifters with long femurs (more knee moment arm to fight in high-bar). Olympic weightlifters with very strong quads sometimes have a smaller gap, occasionally even flipped.

faq.q: Should I test a true 1RM or just trust the calculator?
faq.a: For 90% of lifters in 90% of training blocks: trust the calculator. A true 1RM eats 7–10 days of recovery, needs a 45–60 min warm-up, and carries real injury risk. Reserve direct 1RM testing for **competition day** or **once every 8–12 weeks** if you really want to know. Use 3RM or 5RM retests every 4 weeks otherwise — that's what programs like 5/3/1 and Juggernaut are built around.

faq.q: How long after a 1RM test before I can train hard again?
faq.a: Plan on **5–10 days of reduced volume and intensity** after a true 1RM squat. Day 1–3: walking, mobility, very light bike. Day 4–6: 50–65% bar work, no AMRAPs. Day 7+: ramp back to 75–85% working sets. Ed Coan and Kirk Karwoski training logs both show ~10 days of dialed-back volume after meet attempts in the 800–900 lb range.

faq.q: Does the calculator work the same for paused squats and tempo squats?
faq.a: The math is the same but the inputs aren't comparable. A 3-second paused squat at 315 lb × 5 doesn't predict the same 1RM as touch-and-go 315 × 5 — your paused 1RM is usually **5–8% lower** than your competition or gym 1RM. Run Epley on paused-only data when you're projecting paused competition attempts; mixing rep schemes contaminates the estimate.

faq.q: What if I'm a beginner and don't know my real top set?
faq.a: Don't test a 1RM. Run **Starting Strength** or **StrongLifts 5×5** for 12 weeks, add weight every session, and let your linear progression reveal your starting 5RM. Once you stall on linear progression (usually around bodyweight × 1.2–1.5 squat), plug the last successful 5×5 set into the calculator — that gives you a real, reliable estimated 1RM to build the next program on.
